In [[number theory]], specifically in [[Diophantine approximation]] theory, the '''Markov constant''' <math>M(\alpha)</math> of an [[irrational number]] <math>\alpha</math> is the factor for which [[Dirichlet's approximation theorem]] can be improved for <math>\alpha</math>.

== History and motivation ==
Certain numbers can be approximated well by certain [[Rational number|rationals]]; specifically, the [[Continued fraction#Infinite continued fractions and convergents|convergents of the continued fraction]] are the best [[Diophantine approximation|approximations by rational numbers]] having denominators less than a certain bound. For example, the approximation <math>\pi\approx\frac{22}{7}</math> is the best rational approximation among rational numbers with denominator up to 56.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://oeis.org/A063673|title=A063673 (Denominators of sequence {3/1, 13/4, 16/5, 19/6, 22/7, 179/57, 201/64, 223/71, 245/78, 267/85, 289/92, 311/99, 333/106, ... } of approximations to Pi with increasing denominators, where each approximation is an improvement on its predecessors.) |last=Fernando|first=Suren L.|date=27 July 2001|website=The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|access-date=2 December 2019}}</ref> Also, some numbers can be approximated more readily than others. [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet|Dirichlet]] proved in 1840 that the least readily approximable numbers are the [[Rational number|rational numbers]], in the sense that for every irrational number there exists infinitely many rational numbers approximating it to a certain degree of accuracy that only finitely many such [[Diophantine approximation|rational approximations]] exist for rational numbers. Specifically, he proved that for any number <math>\alpha</math> there are infinitely many pairs of relatively prime numbers <math>(p,q)</math> such that <math>\left|\alpha - \frac{p}{q}\right| < \frac{1}{q^2}</math> if and only if <math>\alpha</math> is irrational.

51 years later, [[Adolf Hurwitz|Hurwitz]] further improved [[Dirichlet's approximation theorem]] by a factor of {{radic|5}},<ref>{{cite journal|last=Hurwitz|first=A.|author-link=Adolf Hurwitz|year=1891|title=Ueber die angenäherte Darstellung der Irrationalzahlen durch rationale Brüche (On the approximate representation of irrational numbers by rational fractions)|journal=[[Mathematische Annalen]]|language=de|url=https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/id/PPN235181684_0039 |volume=39|issue=2|pages=279–284|doi=10.1007/BF01206656|jfm=23.0222.02|s2cid=119535189 }} contains the actual proof in German.</ref> improving the right-hand side from <math>1/q^2</math> to <math>1/\sqrt{5}q^2</math> for irrational numbers:

: <math>\left|\alpha - \frac{p}{q}\right| < \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}q^2}.</math>

The above result is best possible since the [[golden ratio|golden ratio <math>\phi</math>]] is irrational but if we replace {{radic|5}} by any larger number in the above expression then we will only be able to find finitely many rational numbers that satisfy the inequality for <math>\alpha=\phi</math>.

Furthermore, he showed that among the irrational numbers, the least readily approximable numbers are those of the form <math>\frac{a\phi+b}{c\phi+d}</math> where <math>\phi</math> is the [[golden ratio]], <math>a,b,c,d\in\Z</math> and <math>ad-bc=\pm1</math>.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/HurwitzsIrrationalNumberTheorem.html|title=Hurwitz's Irrational Number Theorem|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|date=25 November 2019|website=Wolfram Mathworld|access-date=2 December 2019}}</ref> (These numbers are said to be ''[[Diophantine approximation#Equivalent real numbers|equivalent]]'' to <math>\phi</math>.) If we omit these numbers, just as we omitted the rational numbers in Dirichlet's theorem, then we ''can'' increase the number {{radic|5}} to 2{{radic|2}}.  Again this new bound is best possible in the new setting, but this time the number [[square root of 2|{{radic|2}}]], and numbers equivalent to it, limits the bound.<ref name=":1" /> If we don't allow those numbers then we ''can'' again increase the number on the right hand side of the inequality from 2{{radic|2}} to {{radic|221}}/5,<ref name=":1" /> for which the numbers equivalent to <math>\frac{1+\sqrt{221}}{10}</math> limit the bound. The numbers generated show how well these numbers can be approximated; this can be seen as a property of the real numbers.

However, instead of considering Hurwitz's theorem (and the extensions mentioned above) as a property of the real numbers except certain special numbers, we can consider it as a property of each excluded number. Thus, the theorem can be interpreted as "numbers equivalent to <math>\phi</math>, {{radic|2}} or <math>\frac{1+\sqrt{221}}{10}</math> are among the least readily approximable irrational numbers." This leads us to consider how accurately each number can be approximated by rationals - specifically, by how much can the factor in [[Dirichlet's approximation theorem]] be increased to from 1 for ''that specific'' number.

== Definition ==
Mathematically, the Markov constant of irrational <math>\alpha</math> is defined as <math>M(\alpha)=\sup \left\{\lambda\in\R : \left\vert \alpha - \frac{p}{q} \right\vert<\frac{1}{\lambda q^2} \text{ has infinitely many solutions for }p,q\in\N \right\}</math>.<ref name="WLV">{{Cite book|title=Fundamentals of Number Theory|last=LeVeque|first=William|publisher=Addison-Wesley Publishing Company, Inc.|year=1977|isbn=0-201-04287-8|pages=251–254}}</ref> If the set does not have an upper bound we define <math>M(\alpha)=\infty</math>.

Alternatively, it can be defined as <math>\limsup_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{k^2\left\vert \alpha-\frac{f(k)}{k} \right\vert}</math> where <math>f(k)</math> is defined as the closest integer to <math>\alpha k</math>.

== Properties and results ==
[[Hurwitz's theorem (number theory)|Hurwitz's theorem]] implies that <math>M(\alpha)\ge\sqrt{5}</math> for all <math>\alpha\in\R-\Q</math>.

If <math>\alpha = [a_0; a_1, a_2, ...]</math> is its [[continued fraction]] expansion then <math>M(\alpha)=\limsup_{k\to\infty}{([a_{k+1}; a_{k+2}, a_{k+3}, ...] + [0; a_{k}, a_{k-1}, ...,a_2,a_1])}</math>.<ref name="WLV" />

From the above, if <math>p=\limsup_{k\to\infty}{a_k}</math> then <math>p<M(\alpha)<p+2</math>. This implies that <math>M(\alpha)=\infty</math> if and only if [[Restricted partial quotients|<math>(a_k)</math> is not bounded]]. In particular, <math>M(\alpha)<\infty</math> if <math>\alpha</math> is a [[quadratic irrational number]]. In fact, the lower bound for <math>M(\alpha)</math> can be strengthened to <math>M(\alpha)\ge\sqrt{p^2+4}</math>, the tightest possible.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hancl|first=Jaroslav|date=January 2016|title=Second basic theorem of Hurwitz|journal=Lithuanian Mathematical Journal|volume=56|pages=72–76|doi=10.1007/s10986-016-9305-4|s2cid=124639896 }}</ref>

The values of <math>\alpha</math> for which <math>M(\alpha)<3</math> are families of quadratic irrationalities having the same period (but at different offsets), and the values of <math>M(\alpha)</math> for these <math>\alpha</math> are limited to [[Lagrange number|Lagrange numbers]]. There are [[Uncountable set|uncountably]] many numbers for which <math>M(\alpha)=3</math>, no two of which have the same ending; for instance, for each number <math>\alpha = [\underbrace{1;1,...,1}_{r_1},2,2,\underbrace{1,1,...,1}_{r_2},2,2,\underbrace{1,1,...,1}_{r_3},2,2,...]</math> where <math>r_1<r_2<r_3<\cdots</math>, <math>M(\alpha)=3</math>.<ref name="WLV" />

If <math>\beta=\frac{p\alpha+q}{r\alpha+s}</math> where <math>p,q,r,s\in\Z</math> then <math>M(\beta)\ge\frac{M(\alpha)}{\left\vert ps-rq \right\vert}</math>.<ref name="ar1">{{Cite journal|arxiv=1510.02407|title=Markov constant and quantum instabilities|journal=Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical|volume=49|issue=15|article-number=155201|doi=10.1088/1751-8113/49/15/155201|year=2016|last1=Pelantová|first1=Edita|last2=Starosta|first2=Štěpán|last3=Znojil|first3=Miloslav|bibcode=2016JPhA...49o5201P|s2cid=119161523 }} </ref> In particular if <math>\left\vert ps-rq \right\vert=1     </math> then <math>M(\beta)=M(\alpha)     </math>.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=[[Encyclopaedia of Mathematics]]|last=Hazewinkel|first=Michiel|author-link=Michiel Hazewinkel|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|year=1990|isbn=978-1-55608-005-0|pages=106}}</ref>

The set <math>L=\{M(\alpha)\mid\alpha\in\R-\Q\}</math> forms the [[Markov spectrum#Lagrange spectrum|Lagrange spectrum]]. It contains the interval <math>[F,\infty]</math> where ''F'' is Freiman's constant.<ref name=":0" /> Hence, if <math>m>F\approx4.52783</math> then there exists irrational <math>\alpha</math> whose Markov constant is <math>m</math>.

=== Numbers having a Markov constant less than 3 ===
Burger et al. (2002)<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burger|first1=Edward B.|last2=Folsom|first2=Amanda|last3=Pekker|first3=Alexander|last4=Roengpitya|first4=Rungporn|last5=Snyder|first5=Julia|date=2002|title=On a quantitative refinement of the Lagrange spectrum|journal=Acta Arithmetica|volume=102|issue=1|pages=59–60|bibcode=2002AcAri.102...55B|doi=10.4064/aa102-1-5|doi-access=free}}</ref> provides a formula for which the quadratic irrationality <math>\alpha_n
</math> whose Markov constant is the n<sup>th</sup> [[Lagrange number]]:

<math>\alpha_n=\frac{2u-3m_n+\sqrt{9m_n^2-4}}{2m_n}</math> where <math>m_n</math> is the n<sup>th</sup> [[Markov number]], and {{Mvar|u}} is the smallest positive integer such that <math>m_n\mid u^2+1</math>.

Nicholls (1978)<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nicholls|first=Peter|date=1978|title=Diophantine Approximation via the Modular Group|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |series=Second Series|volume=17|pages=11–17|doi=10.1112/jlms/s2-17.1.11}}</ref> provides a geometric proof of this (based on circles tangent to each other), providing a method that these numbers can be systematically found.

=== Markov constant of two numbers ===
Since <math>\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}=[1;\overline{1,1,2}]</math>,

: <math>\begin{align} M\left ( \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2} \right )
& = \max([1;\overline{2,1,1}]+[0;\overline{1,2,1}],[1;\overline{1,2,1}]+[0;\overline{2,1,1}],[2;\overline{1,1,2}]+[0;\overline{1,1,2}]) \\
& = \max\left ( \frac{2\sqrt{10}}{3},\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{3},\sqrt{10} \right ) \\
& = \sqrt{10}. \end{align}     </math>

As <math>
  e = [2; 1, 2, 1, 1, 4, 1, 1, 6, 1, \ldots, 1, 2n, 1, \ldots], M(e)=\infty
</math> because the [[E (mathematical constant)#Representations|continued fraction representation of {{Mvar|e}}]] is unbounded.

=== Numbers &alpha;<sub>n</sub> having Markov constant less than 3 ===
Consider <math>n=6</math>; Then <math>m_n=34</math>. By trial and error it can be found that <math>u=13</math>. Then

: <math>\begin{align} \alpha_6 & = \frac{2u-3m_6+\sqrt{9m_6^2-4}}{2m_6} \\[6pt]
& = \frac{-76+\sqrt{10400}}{68} \\[6pt]
&= \frac{-19+5\sqrt{26}}{17} \\[6pt]
&=[0;\overline{2,1,1,1,1,1,1,2}]. \end{align}</math>
